coverage.note: Checked tier isolation, the agent backup, token revocation, admin roles and Admin API auth, cache isolation, anonymisation and audit.
Checked async write failure semantics, MMP dependency, cache staleness, vector capacity and recovery.
Checked DR/monitoring ownership, DPO decisions, cost scope and admin governance.

doc_anchors.quote: the agent backup survives learner deletion of their own memory (enabling session resume)
Each agent shall maintain its own per-learner backup memory, used only when the learner namespace is
Learners shall be able to request deletion of their own user-deletable memory.

evidence.quote: the agent backup survives learner deletion of their own memory (enabling session resume)
Learners shall be able to request deletion of their own user-deletable memory.
HIGHLY_RESTRICTED data shall be stored in a physically separate schema (memory_sensitive) with

A backup that copies namespace content, has no stated tier or credentials, and is kept after learner deletion means deleted or HIGHLY_RESTRICTED data lives on outside the controls that NFR-5, FR-15 and FR-13 require.

next_step.action: Decide the backup retention and deletion policy, then specify the backup storage tier in Section 13.
next_step.owner: Data Protection Officer with platform architect

recommendation.change_summary: Add a subsection to Section 13 that does four things. (a) Put backup records in the same standard or sensitive schema split, so counselling backup goes in memory_sensitive. (b) Route reads of the backup through the Auditor with source=backup. (c) Make FR-15 deletion cascade to every agent's backup for user-deletable keys, replacing the 'survives learner deletion' property. (d) Set a backup retention ceiling. Add test cases to FR-15 and NFR-5 that cover the backup.
recommendation.expected_benefit: FR-15 deletion and NFR-5 isolation then cover every copy of learner data, and P7 audit covers backup reads.
recommendation.issue: The agent backup store has no storage tier, credentials, retention, audit or deletion rules, and is kept on purpose after a learner deletes their memory.
recommendation.rationale: Without these rules, the backup is an ungoverned copy of learner personal data, including counselling data.
recommendation.verification: Extend the FR-15 deletion boundary test to check that agent backups no longer hold the deleted keys. Extend the NFR-5 test so a standard credential cannot read the counselling agent's backup.

findings.statement: Section 13 and FR-16 give every agent a per-learner backup store that holds copies of namespace content, including the counselling agent's copy of HIGHLY_RESTRICTED data. The document says nowhere which schema or credentials this store uses, how it is encrypted, how long it is kept, or how it is audited. It also says the backup deliberately survives a learner's own deletion. As written, the backup gets around the NFR-5 tier separation, the FR-15 deletion right, the P7 audit-everything principle and the Gateway's pre-retrieval checks. That is a personal-data exposure under the PDPA obligations the design cites.
findings.title: Agent per-learner backup sits outside the governed tiers and survives learner deletion

doc_anchors.quote: On revocation: inform the learner, serve from agent backup only, no re-authentication path is offered.
Auth tokens shall be valid for 48 hours, with defined degraded-mode behaviour for EXPIRED and REVOKED

evidence.quote: On revocation: inform the learner, serve from agent backup only, no re-authentication path is offered.
Revoking a token without cutting off the backup leaves learner data available to the session the revocation was meant to stop.

next_step.action: Decide whether any learner-specific memory may be served after revocation, and record the decision in Section 25.

recommendation.change_summary: Change the Section 15 Check 3 REVOKED branch to deny all learner-specific memory, backup included. Serve only agent-global content and log the attempt. Update Section 6 and the Section 25 decision text to match. Add an NFR-6 test step that confirms no backup content is returned under REVOKED.
recommendation.expected_benefit: NFR-6 revocation then actually stops access, and the P2 private-by-default principle is protected.
recommendation.issue: Under REVOKED status the agent still serves learner data from its backup.
recommendation.rationale: Revocation should end access to personal data. Only the learner's own non-sensitive session continuity could justify any exception, and that needs an explicit policy decision.
recommendation.verification: In the token lifecycle test, revoke a token mid-session and check that the context pack contains no per-learner content.

findings.statement: Sections 6, 15 and 25 say that when a token is REVOKED the agent keeps serving the learner from its backup memory. Revocation normally signals a compromised account, a leaver or a suspended learner. Continuing to serve personal data, including counselling backup for the counselling agent, after revocation defeats the reason for revoking. This refines the confirmed auth-token decision: the issue is what happens on revocation, not the 48-hour window.
findings.title: A revoked token still gets learner data served from the agent backup

doc_anchors.quote: failed writes queue and retry automatically; multiple independent consumers (audit, embedding, SIS sync) read the same event stream
processed asynchronously by a background consumer performing classify → embed → validate → route →

evidence.quote: failed writes queue and retry automatically; multiple independent consumers (audit, embedding, SIS sync) read the same event stream
processed asynchronously by a background consumer performing classify → embed → validate → route →

Validation runs after the ACK and there is no dead-letter or notification path, so rejected writes are either lost silently or retried without end. Embedding also runs before validation, so rejected content is still sent to the embedding service.

recommendation.change_summary: In Section 18: (1) split failures into transient ones (retry with backoff and a maximum attempt count) and deterministic ones (validation or policy rejection, sent straight to a per-tier dead-letter topic, audited, and shown on the MMP dashboard); (2) run validation before embedding; (3) require a client-side sensitivity declaration at the Gateway, and have a standard consumer that classifies content as HIGHLY_RESTRICTED quarantine it rather than store it; (4) define an idempotency key and per-learner/slot partitioning.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Writes stay reliable under FR-9 and tier isolation holds in transit under NFR-5.
recommendation.issue: Section 18 has no failure semantics for writes that are rejected after the ACK, and topic routing comes before classification.
recommendation.rationale: Writes lost silently undermine P1, because the namespace stops being authoritative. Misrouted sensitive content undermines P4 and NFR-5.
recommendation.verification: Add FR-9 and FR-11 test cases: a strict-mode rejection appears in the dead-letter topic and the audit log exactly once, and a replayed message does not create a duplicate record.

findings.statement: The agent receives an ACK as soon as its write is enqueued. Classify, embed and validate all run later in the consumer, yet the document defines no outcome for writes the Validator rejects in strict mode. Agents and learners are never told, and 'retry automatically' would retry deterministic rejections forever unless there is a dead-letter path. The tier topic (standard or sensitive) is picked at the Gateway before Classify confirms sensitivity, so content that classification upgrades has already gone through the standard topic and the standard embedding deployment. Idempotency and per-slot ordering under retry are also not specified.
findings.title: Async write path: no path for writes rejected after the ACK, no dead-letter handling, and the topic is chosen before classification

request/response JSON schemas and auth on the Admin API itself are not yet specified
wellbeing/counselling/ shall be classified HIGHLY_RESTRICTED with zero cross-domain reads and no

evidence.quote: Super Admin Everything - always audit-logged, mandatory reason required
Super admin Overrides, corrections, emergency access (always audit-logged)
request/response JSON schemas and auth on the Admin API itself are not yet specified
A Super Admin with 'Everything' and override rights through an Admin API with no defined auth is an MMP override path into counselling, which FR-5 forbids.

recommendation.change_summary: Amend Section 19 so Super Admin covers everything except memory_sensitive. Give the MMP service no memory_sensitive credentials. Add an Admin API auth subsection to Section 21: Entra ID roles per endpoint, a mandatory reason for learner-level reads, and least-privilege access to the audit endpoints. Extend the FR-5 test to attempt counselling reads with Super Admin and MMP credentials.
recommendation.expected_benefit: The FR-5 hard wall becomes something the design actually enforces, and the FR-14 API is secured.
recommendation.issue: Admin roles and the Admin API leave open an override path into counselling and have no auth model.
recommendation.rationale: FR-5 and P4 require that no MMP override path exists, enforced at the credential level.
recommendation.verification: FR-5 test: reads of counselling data through the Super Admin role and the MMP service credential are both denied.

findings.statement: Section 19 gives Super Admin access to 'Everything', and Section 21 lists Super Admin 'Overrides ... emergency access' through the MMP. FR-5 and P4 forbid any MMP override path to wellbeing/counselling/. The Admin API, which exposes per-learner audit logs and slot DELETE, has no authentication or authorisation model yet. Section 28 acknowledges this as a code-generation gap. This review adds that it is a security exposure: the API's own auth model has to state that counselling is excluded from override.
findings.title: Super Admin and MMP 'overrides' conflict with the counselling hard wall, and Admin API auth is undefined

doc_anchors.quote: Not exists + auto-provisionable slot type -> MMP provisions slot, proceed
MMP downtime shall not affect agent read or write availability, because the MMP is not in the critical

evidence.quote: Not exists + auto-provisionable slot type -> MMP provisions slot, proceed
+-- AuditStore -- append-only log of every operation
Synchronous MMP provisioning and an AuditStore hosted in the MMP make MMP availability a dependency of agent reads and writes, which contradicts NFR-4.

recommendation.change_summary: In Sections 15 and 21, state that the AuditStore is a separately deployed append-only sink, fed by the Kafka audit consumer and independent of MMP uptime. Make Check 4 auto-provisioning either a Gateway-local operation using cached templates, or a deny-and-retry with a defined reason code. Extend the NFR-4 chaos test to cover a first write to an unprovisioned module slot and audit completeness while the MMP is down.
recommendation.expected_benefit: NFR-4 availability holds with no loss of FR-13 audit completeness.
recommendation.issue: Check 4 provisioning and audit storage depend on the MMP service.
recommendation.rationale: NFR-4 and FR-13 cannot both hold if the AuditStore is down along with the MMP.
recommendation.verification: NFR-4 chaos test with the MMP stopped: an auto-provisionable write succeeds or is deterministically denied, and the audit log has every entry once the test ends.

findings.statement: NFR-4 relies on the MMP being outside the critical path. But Gateway Check 4 calls on the MMP to provision missing slots during a request, and the AuditStore that the mandatory Auditor writes to is listed as an MMP component. If the MMP is down, either requests that need auto-provisioning fail and audited operations block, or audit entries are lost, which breaks FR-13. The design does not say which.
findings.title: MMP is in the request path for slot auto-provisioning and audit storage, contrary to NFR-4

doc_anchors.quote: Policy decisions are not cached - they are evaluated fresh on every request, so that a rule change takes effect immediately
context pack is cached so repeated queries within a session skip PostgreSQL entirely

evidence.quote: Policy decisions are not cached - they are evaluated fresh on every request, so that a rule change takes effect immediately
context pack is cached so repeated queries within a session skip PostgreSQL entirely
The cached pack contains content that was redacted and permitted earlier, so a rule change or deletion only takes effect at the next session, which contradicts the 'immediately' claim.

recommendation.change_summary: In Section 18, add cache invalidation triggered by policy changes, slot permission changes, learner deletions and slot expiry. Key cache entries by agent_id and policy version. Either exclude HIGHLY_RESTRICTED content from the shared Redis cache or use a separate cache instance with separate credentials. Add an FR-10 test step.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Policy changes and deletions take effect immediately for FR-8 and FR-15, and NFR-5 isolation covers the cache.
recommendation.issue: Cached context packs bypass the guarantee that policy changes and deletions take effect immediately, and the cache is not tier-isolated.
recommendation.rationale: FR-8 redaction, recall and deletion dimensions and NFR-5 isolation have to apply to cached copies as well.
recommendation.verification: FR-10 test: change a slot read permission mid-session, and the next read is a cache MISS that returns DENIED.

findings.statement: Section 16 says policy is evaluated fresh so that rule changes take effect immediately. But a cache HIT serves a context pack that was ranked, budgeted and redacted under earlier policy, and it is invalidated only at session close or token expiry. Permission revocations, learner deletions and redaction changes are therefore not reflected for the rest of the session. The Redis cache is also not split by sensitivity tier, so HIGHLY_RESTRICTED context packs for the counselling agent may sit in a shared cache outside the separate-credential boundary of NFR-5.
findings.title: Cached context packs keep serving after permission changes, deletions or redaction updates, and the Redis cache has no tier isolation

doc_anchors.quote: Queries are always filtered by learner_id + slot_path - the effective search space per query is 500-800 vectors, not 9.5 million.
Azure SKU required Memory Optimised, 16 vCores, 128 GB RAM

evidence.quote: Raw vector storage (1536-dim, 9.5M) ~57 GB
Azure SKU required Memory Optimised, 16 vCores, 128 GB RAM
57 GB of vectors plus an 80 GB index is about 137 GB, which is more than 128 GB of RAM, so the in-RAM assumption behind NFR-2 is not shown to hold.
p95 filtered similarity query latency ≤ 15 ms, p50 ≤ 10 ms, measured against

next_step.action: Build and run the synthetic 9.5M-vector benchmark on the Memory Optimised 16-vCore SKU.

recommendation.change_summary: Before Build Phase 5, run a prototype benchmark on the confirmed SKU with 9.5M synthetic vectors spread across both schemas. Measure p50/p95 latency, recall@k for filters with few matching rows (500-800 rows), and buffer cache hit ratio. Add recall and memory-residency thresholds to the NFR-2 acceptance criterion. Record a contingency, such as partitioning by learner or a B-tree-first exact search for small per-learner sets.
recommendation.expected_benefit: NFR-2 latency and NFR-10 cost are confirmed early, before the confirmed SKU is locked in.
recommendation.issue: Memory fit and filtered-search behaviour at 9.5M vectors are asserted, not measured.
recommendation.rationale: NFR-1, NFR-2 and NFR-10 all depend on the SKU sizing.
recommendation.verification: Benchmark report shows p95 ≤ 15 ms with recall@10 at or above an agreed threshold.

findings.statement: Section 12 sizes about 57 GB of raw vectors plus an 80 GB HNSW index against a 128 GB RAM SKU. The two together exceed RAM before counting the event and document tables or the second schema, which undermines the 'in-RAM index' basis for the 5-15 ms latency target. Section 12 also says filtering cuts the effective search space to 500-800 vectors, but a single global HNSW index is built over all vectors. Whether filters with very few matching rows keep both latency and recall depends on how the query is executed. That is unverified here and needs measuring.
findings.title: pgvector memory fit and the filtered-HNSW search-space claim need a benchmark

doc_anchors.quote: MMP in detail - template versioning conflict resolution, SIS integration failure handling.
Learner namespace is authoritative - the agent's copy is backup only. Conflicts are resolved in favour

evidence.quote: MMP in detail - template versioning conflict resolution, SIS integration failure handling.
Learner namespace is authoritative - the agent's copy is backup only. Conflicts are resolved in favour
An authoritative store with no stated backup, RPO/RTO or pipeline monitoring has no defined recovery from data loss or a stalled consumer.

next_step.action: Propose RPO/RTO and availability targets for approval, and assign on-call ownership.

recommendation.change_summary: Add an Operations section setting out: PostgreSQL HA and point-in-time-restore with stated RPO/RTO; how backup retention handles learner deletion; alerts on consumer lag, dead-letter count, unembedded backlog and SIS webhook failures; and a named on-call owner. Add matching NFR rows and Section 27 criteria.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Recovery is defined for P1/FR-9, and backups stay consistent with FR-15.
recommendation.issue: Recovery and operational monitoring are not specified.
recommendation.rationale: Losing the authoritative namespace, or a stalled consumer going unnoticed, would break P1 and FR-9 for every agent.
recommendation.verification: Restore drill meets the stated RTO, and a simulated consumer stall raises an alert within the agreed threshold.

findings.statement: The learner namespace is authoritative (P1), yet the document gives no PostgreSQL backup, high availability, RPO/RTO or availability SLO. It also sets no alerting for Kafka consumer lag, dead-letter growth or SIS webhook failures. SIS integration failure handling is acknowledged in the backlog. This review adds that DR and monitoring need an owner and targets before build, and that backups have to be reconciled with FR-15 deletion.
findings.title: No backup/DR, availability targets or operational monitoring for the authoritative store and pipeline

doc_anchors.quote: Memory Router Component 5 (Auditor) - log schema detail, retention period, PDPA alignment sign-off.
Private by default - memory is private to the learner, shared by exception, anonymised for service

evidence.quote: Memory Router Component 5 (Auditor) - log schema detail, retention period, PDPA alignment sign-off.
Private by default - memory is private to the learner, shared by exception, anonymised for service
With no anonymisation method or minimum group size, cohort-level patterns readable by every agent could re-identify learners in small cohorts.

next_step.action: Approve the anonymisation rule and the audit retention period.

recommendation.change_summary: Add to Section 19 a defined anonymisation rule: which sensitivity tiers are excluded, a minimum aggregation group size, and an owner. Have the DPO set the audit retention period in Section 17 before Build Phase 4. Add a test that cohort aggregates below the minimum group size are suppressed.
recommendation.expected_benefit: The P2 and FR-13/NFR-7 PDPA obligations rest on signed-off rules.
recommendation.issue: Anonymisation and audit retention are assumed compliant, with no decision owner.
recommendation.rationale: P2 and P7 compliance depend on these choices.
recommendation.verification: DPO sign-off is recorded in Section 25, and the aggregate suppression test passes.

findings.statement: Cross-learner and cohort patterns are said to be 'anonymised' and are readable by all agents. No anonymisation method or minimum group size is defined, and RESTRICTED data (at-risk flags, financial aid, accessibility) is excluded only implicitly. Audit retention and PDPA alignment sign-off are acknowledged as pending. This review adds that both should be decided by the DPO before agents start writing pattern data or audit logs build up, because both decisions affect what gets stored.
findings.title: Anonymisation standard, audit retention and PDPA sign-off have no accountable decision

doc_anchors.quote: Vector-store infrastructure cost shall remain within the SGD 800-1,200/month estimate at 15,000-learner
computed from the actual provisioned Azure SKU and measured embedding volume, falls within SGD

evidence.quote: Vector-store infrastructure cost shall remain within the SGD 800-1,200/month estimate at 15,000-learner
computed from the actual provisioned Azure SKU and measured embedding volume, falls within SGD

recommendation.change_summary: Split NFR-10 into a vector-store line and a total-platform line (PostgreSQL, Event Hubs, Redis, both embedding deployments, audit storage), each with its own budget and an owner. Align the Section 27 test to match.
recommendation.expected_benefit: NFR-10 becomes verifiable and covers the full run cost.
recommendation.issue: Cost requirement and its test have different scopes, and the total platform cost is not bounded.
recommendation.rationale: Operators need a single total cost envelope to monitor against the MMP cost dashboard.
recommendation.verification: Cost model check reports each line against its own budget.

findings.statement: NFR-10 limits only 'vector-store infrastructure' cost to SGD 800-1,200/month. The acceptance test computes cost from the SKU plus measured embedding volume. Event Hubs, Redis, the separate sensitive embedding deployment and audit storage are outside both. The cost envelope that governance needs is therefore incomplete and is measured inconsistently.
findings.title: NFR-10 cost scope covers only the vector store, while its test includes embedding volume

doc_anchors.quote: separate topics per sensitivity tier keep HIGHLY_RESTRICTED writes physically isolated in transit
A credential valid for memory_standard is confirmed to fail authentication against memory_sensitive, and vice versa.

evidence.quote: separate topics per sensitivity tier keep HIGHLY_RESTRICTED writes physically isolated in transit
A credential valid for memory_standard is confirmed to fail authentication against memory_sensitive, and vice versa.

findings.no_change_rationale: Enforcing isolation at the credential level and in transit meets FR-5 and NFR-5 as written, and the acceptance test checks it directly.
findings.statement: HIGHLY_RESTRICTED data has its own schema with separate credentials and a separate embedding deployment. Its writes go through a dedicated Kafka topic, and NFR-5 has a test that checks credentials fail across tiers. This puts the FR-5/P4 hard wall at the credential level, not only in policy logic. FND-001 and FND-006 extend the same boundary to the backup and the cache.
findings.title: Two-tier sensitive storage with separate credentials and per-tier topics

doc_anchors.quote: Access control is pre-retrieval. The namespace check gates the query itself - not the returned results.

sound_areas.why_sound: The ordered six-check Gateway denies on any failure and logs a reason code, which gives the pre-retrieval control and auditability that FR-4 and P3 require. The FR-4 test checks each check on its own.

sound_areas.why_sound: The Auditor's log fields include source (namespace, backup or global) and it covers cache hits and enqueues, which supports the FR-13 audit trail. Retention is a separate pending item (FND-009).

doc_anchors.quote: Fallback path (embedding service unavailable):

sound_areas.why_sound: The embedding fallback flags records as unembedded, uses BM25 for retrieval and queues them for re-embedding. This keeps reads available when the embedding service is down, and the MMP backlog dashboard makes the gap visible to operators.
